title: The Numbered Sayings
hookLine: teachings arranged from ones to elevens

lines: A NUMBER GIVES THE MIND A SHELF.
cards: Three things to pack for a trip. Five steps to a calmer morning. Seven habits.
Ten rules. A number in the title gives the mind a shelf. You know when you've got them all.
You notice when one is missing. The monks who carried the Buddha's teaching by memory knew that too.
They gathered a whole collection of discourses and sorted them, not by topic or by place, but by how many items each one listed.

teach.b: The Anguttara Nikaya is the fourth of the great collections of discourses in the Pali canon, after the Long, the Middle-Length and the Connected. Its name is usually explained as increasing by one factor.
It has eleven books. The Book of Ones holds teachings about one thing. The Book of Twos, two things.

And so on, all the way up to the Book of Elevens. There are a great many discourses, most of them short, and many repeat a pattern with small changes, which is how memorizers worked. Why arrange it this way?

teach.h: A NUMBERED LIST IS A HANDRAIL
teach.b: Partly memory: in an oral tradition, a numbered list is a handrail. If you're reciting the five hindrances and only reach four, you know to look again.
And partly use: a monk asked to teach about, say, three things to watch could go straight to the Threes. Here's a real three, from the Book of Threes, paraphrased.
There are three marks of anything conditioned, anything put together.
Its arising is seen. Its passing away is seen. And while it lasts, its changing is seen.
That's the whole discourse. You could say it on one breath, and it's enough to look at a cup of tea, a mood, or a friendship.
Over the next weeks come some well-known pages of the Anguttara: a mind that shines, a talk to a doubtful village, a gold-washer, a lump of salt.
The numbers are just shelves. The teachings are what sits on them.

how: Theravada monastics and lay students study the Anguttara Nikaya alongside the other collections, and many teachers draw on its numbered lists for talks to lay communities.

games.q: you're a monk in an oral tradition, asked to teach about three things to watch. where in the Anguttara do you look?
games.why: the collection is shelved by number, so a teaching on three things sits in the Book of Threes.

practice: Bring to mind something simple near you, a cup, a plant, the light in the room, your own breath, and read one three with it.
First its arising: it came to be, at some point, from something; then its passing: it will end, or is ending already.
Last, while it lasts, its changing: watch for the small shifts, even now, and let arising, passing, changing rest in the mind as you breathe.
